recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble portrait shows NGC 1309, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Eridanus. NASA has given its distance as both 100 million and 110 million light-years. Hubble photographed the galaxy in 2005, 2006 and 2010, years before a weak supernova appeared in it.

That explosion, SN 2012Z, was spotted by the Lick Observatory Supernova Search in January 2012. It belongs to Type Iax, a recently identified class of exploding white dwarfs that are fainter and less energetic than Type Ia supernovae. Curtis McCully of Rutgers sharpened the older Hubble images and found an object at the supernova's position, the first time astronomers had spotted the system behind such a blast.

The team thinks the object is most likely a blue companion star stripped down to its helium core. The white dwarf slowly drew fuel from it until a runaway nuclear reaction set off the explosion, which is thought to leave a battered white dwarf behind, nicknamed a zombie star.

understand.summary: A composite from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F435W is shown in blue, F555W in green and F814W in red.
understand.eye: The F814W filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see, and Hubble's sharpness let astronomers pick out a single star system in a galaxy this far away.

explore: The chance that the object is an unrelated star lined up by coincidence is less than one percent. The team still could not rule out other explanations, including a single massive star that exploded, and planned to look again with Hubble in 2015, once the supernova had faded. More than 30 Type Iax supernovae had been identified by then.
sources: NASA release: NASA’s Hubble Finds Supernova Star System Linked to Potential ‘Zombie Star’
